questions.title: What is SAP Gateway, what is its purpose, and what are its main use cases?
questions.description: SAP Gateway is the technology that exposes data and business logic from SAP ABAP systems (like SAP S/4HANA or SAP ERP) as OData services over HTTP, so that any client, above all SAPUI5 and SAP Fiori apps, can use them with standard web technology instead of SAP-specific protocols like RFC. Its purpose is to decouple the modern UI from the ABAP back end: the UI only speaks OData (REST over HTTP with JSON or XML), and the Gateway translates these requests into ABAP calls, and the results back into OData. It consists of two parts: the back-end component (IWBEP), where the services are implemented, and the hub or front-end server component (IWFND), where services are registered and called. They can run in the same system (embedded deployment) or in a separate front-end server (hub deployment), which also hosts the SAP Fiori launchpad and the UI5 apps. Typical use cases: providing OData services for SAP Fiori and custom UI5 apps; building services with the Service Builder (transaction SEGW), or generating them from CDS views; integrating mobile apps and third-party systems. Useful transactions are /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE (register and activate services), /IWFND/GW_CLIENT (test a service), and /IWFND/ERROR_LOG (analyze errors). In newer systems, the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) creates OData V2 and V4 services, still served through the same Gateway infrastructure. The problem it solves: ABAP data used to be reachable only through SAP-specific protocols (RFC, BAPIs, SAP GUI), which a browser, a mobile app or a third-party system cannot speak. In one sentence: it makes ABAP data consumable by any HTTP client, with no SAP knowledge needed on the client side. Embedded deployment is simpler with fewer hops (common with S/4HANA); a hub gives better isolation and one entry point for several back ends, with more moving parts. In a hub setup, /IWBEP/REG_SERVICE registers the service on the back-end side. /IWFND/GW_CLIENT is the transaction a UI5 developer really uses: send the request directly and see the raw response, which answers "is this my bug or the service's bug?" in a minute.
keyPoints: SAP Gateway exposes ABAP data and logic as OData services over HTTP.
It decouples the UI (OData, JSON/XML) from the ABAP back end (RFC/ABAP calls).
Back-end component IWBEP + hub/front-end component IWFND; embedded or hub deployment.
Use cases: services for Fiori/UI5, mobile and third-party integration; SEGW, /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, GW_CLIENT, ERROR_LOG.
Embedded (simpler, S/4HANA) vs hub (isolation, one entry point). /IWFND/GW_CLIENT answers "UI bug or service bug?".

questions.title: What are the basic key terms of an SAP landscape (SAP system, client/mandant, Gateway, ABAP back end, DB, SADL, CDS, BOPF)?
questions.description: An SAP system is one installation of SAP software, identified by a three-character system ID (SID), like S4D. Landscapes usually have several systems in a row: development, quality assurance (test), and production, connected by transports. Inside one system, a client (in German, Mandant) is a self-contained unit with its own business data, users and customizing, identified by a three-digit number like 100; one system can have several clients (for example for development and for unit tests), while the ABAP code is cross-client (shared by all clients). The ABAP back end is the application server where the business logic runs, written in ABAP. The DB is the database underneath, today mostly SAP HANA. SAP Gateway exposes the back end's data as OData services to UIs. CDS (Core Data Services) is the way to define data models and views in ABAP on SAP HANA: CDS views define what data is read, with joins, associations and calculations pushed down to the database, and carry annotations that also drive the UI (like UI.LineItem). SADL (Service Adaptation Definition Language) is a framework that turns CDS views (or BOPF objects) into OData services with little or no code, translating OData queries efficiently into database queries. BOPF (Business Object Processing Framework) models transactional business objects with their nodes, actions, validations and determinations, including draft handling; it is the predecessor of the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP), which is used for new development. The distinction that matters: client-dependent objects (business data, customizing) exist per client, while client-independent objects (programs, classes, CDS views, BSP applications, Gateway services) are shared by every client, so a UI5 app deployed to DEV client 100 is also visible in client 200, but shows different data. Development happens only in DEV; everything travels by transport to QAS and PRD. The important architectural shift on HANA is code pushdown: instead of reading millions of rows into ABAP and looping, the logic is expressed in CDS views and runs in the database. CDS annotations like @OData.publish: true (expose a view as an OData service) and @UI.lineItem (drive a Fiori elements column) are the direct equivalent of CAP's CDS annotations. RAP, the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model, replaced the SEGW + BOPF combination: behavior definitions and implementations on top of CDS, generating OData V4 (or V2) services; mentioning it shows you know the current direction.
keyPoints: SAP system: one installation (SID); landscapes chain development, quality, and production systems.
Client (Mandant): a unit with its own business data and customizing inside a system; ABAP code is cross-client.
ABAP back end (application server) + DB (mostly SAP HANA) + Gateway (OData for the UI).
CDS: data models/views with annotations; SADL: exposes CDS/BOPF as OData; BOPF: transactional objects (succeeded by RAP).
Client-dependent: data + customizing; client-independent: code, CDS, BSP apps, services (visible in every client).
Code pushdown to HANA via CDS; RAP is the current model (replaces SEGW + BOPF).

questions.title: What is a package, and what is a BSP application?
questions.description: A package (formerly called a development class) groups related development objects in the ABAP repository, like programs, classes, CDS views, OData services, and UI5 apps, similar to a folder or a project. Every object that should be transported belongs to a package. The package is assigned to a software component and a transport layer, which decide whether and where its objects are transported; packages are managed in SE80 or SE21. Objects in the special local package $TMP are not transportable and stay only in the current system, which is useful for experiments. A BSP application (Business Server Pages) is the container in which a UI5 app is stored in an ABAP system. BSP was originally a web technology of its own, but today it is mostly used just as the storage for SAPUI5 apps in the SAPUI5 ABAP repository: all files of the app (Component-preload.js, manifest.json, views, i18n files) are stored in it. Its name is limited to 15 characters, like ZPRODUCTS. A deployed app is served under a URL like /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/sap/zproducts/, through an ICF service that is created for it. The BSP application belongs to a package and is transported like any other object, and the launchpad configuration refers to it to start the app. Customer packages start with Z or Y and are assigned to a real transport layer. The classic mistake: deploying a UI5 app to $TMP "just to test" and then discovering it cannot be transported to QAS. The BSP name is declared in the manifest under sap.platform.abap.uri. The ICF node must be active (transaction SICF); an inactive node gives a 404 even though the app is deployed correctly, a classic lost afternoon. You can see the BSP application in SE80 with its folder structure intact.
keyPoints: A package groups related development objects; it decides transport through its software component and layer.
$TMP is the local, non-transportable package.
A BSP application is the container that stores a UI5 app in the ABAP repository (name max. 15 characters).
It is served at /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/sap/<name>/ and transported like other objects.
Customer packages Z*/Y*; $TMP objects never reach QAS. An inactive ICF node (SICF) gives a 404.

questions.title: How do the download and upload reports in SE38 work for UI5 apps?
questions.description: Transaction SE38 (the ABAP editor) runs reports, and SAP provides the report /UI5/UI5_REPOSITORY_LOAD to move UI5 apps between a local folder and the SAPUI5 ABAP repository. With it, you can upload an app from a local folder (usually the dist folder after a build) into a BSP application, either creating a new BSP application or updating an existing one; you choose the package and a transport request, so the upload can be transported to other systems. You can also download an existing BSP application to a local folder, for example to look at what is deployed or to start working on it, and you can delete an app from the repository. The report checks the files, handles text encoding and recalculates the app index for the uploaded app. There is also a variant for uploading from a URL. This manual route was common before modern tools; today, apps are usually deployed with SAP Fiori tools (npx fiori deploy, configured with the deploy-to-abap middleware), with the UI5 tooling, or from CI pipelines, which use the same ABAP repository services in the background, but the report is still useful for quick manual uploads, downloads, and troubleshooting. Always run a test run first: it lists which files would be added, changed or deleted, which is your last chance to notice you are overwriting the wrong app. If the launchpad still shows the old version afterwards, recalculate the app index with /UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE. Downloading is also the recovery path when the source was lost, or to compare what really runs in a system with your repository. /UI5/UI5_REPOSITORY_LOAD_HTTP loads from a URL instead of a local folder. The report is what runs underneath fiori deploy, and it is the fallback when the tooling fails.
keyPoints: SE38 runs the report /UI5/UI5_REPOSITORY_LOAD.
Upload: a local folder (like dist) into a new or existing BSP application, with package and transport request.
Download: a deployed BSP application to a local folder; delete is also possible.
Today usually replaced by SAP Fiori tools deploy (deploy-to-abap) or CI, but still handy for manual tasks.
Test run first; recalculate the app index if the launchpad shows the old version; _HTTP variant loads from a URL.

examples.title: Uploading with the report (steps)
examples.code:
1. SE38 -> program /UI5/UI5_REPOSITORY_LOAD -> Execute
2. Choose "Upload", enter the BSP application name (for example ZPRODUCTS)
3. Select the local folder (the build result in dist/)
4. Enter description, package (ZSALES_UI) and transport request
5. Confirm the list of files -> the app is uploaded and the app index is recalculated

questions.title: How do you clear caches when a deployed UI5 app does not show the latest changes?
questions.description: After deploying a new version, users sometimes still see the old app, because several layers keep caches. Work from the outside in. Browser: clear the browser cache or do a hard reload (and, for a deployed app, check that the Component-preload.js was rebuilt). UI5 app index: run the report /UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE (in SE38) for the app, so the server knows about the new files and their versions; this also matters for the cache buster. SAP Fiori launchpad: run /UI2/INVALIDATE_GLOBAL_CACHES to invalidate the launchpad's caches (on the front-end server), and users can clear their own cached launchpad data. ICM / HTTP server cache: in transaction SMICM, choose Goto > HTTP Server Cache > Invalidate > Global (or local), so the web server does not deliver cached files. OData metadata: if the service's metadata changed, clear the Gateway metadata caches with /IWFND/CACHE_CLEANUP on the front-end server and /IWBEP/CACHE_CLEANUP on the back end, otherwise the app may get an outdated $metadata. When the app is set up with the cache buster correctly, most of these steps happen automatically after a proper deployment. The app index is the one people forget: the launchpad reads it to find applications and their manifests, so after a deployment it must be up to date (it can also run as a scheduled job). /UI2/DELETE_CACHE_AFTER_IMP is the equivalent launchpad cache step after a transport import; the exact set of UI2 cache reports differs by release. In the browser, sap-ui-xx-componentPreload=off and sap-ui-debug=true help to see the newest single files. The order to work through when an app looks stale: browser → app index → UI2 / launchpad caches → Gateway metadata. Saying that sequence is a better answer than listing transactions, because it shows you have actually debugged it. The cache buster puts a changing token into resource URLs (~1234567890~), so browsers can cache files forever and still get new versions right after a deployment.
keyPoints: Browser cache: hard reload, and make sure the preload was rebuilt.
/UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE recalculates the app index (also needed for the cache buster).
/UI2/INVALIDATE_GLOBAL_CACHES for the launchpad; SMICM > HTTP Server Cache > Invalidate for the ICM.
OData metadata: /IWFND/CACHE_CLEANUP (front end) and /IWBEP/CACHE_CLEANUP (back end).
Order: browser → app index → UI2 caches → Gateway metadata. After imports: /UI2/DELETE_CACHE_AFTER_IMP.

examples.title: Cache layers and what clears them
examples.code:
Browser cache                  -> hard reload / clear browser data
UI5 app index                  -> SE38: /UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE
Fiori launchpad caches         -> SE38: /UI2/INVALIDATE_GLOBAL_CACHES
ICM HTTP server cache          -> SMICM: Goto > HTTP Server Cache > Invalidate > Global
Gateway metadata (front end)   -> /IWFND/CACHE_CLEANUP
Gateway metadata (back end)    -> /IWBEP/CACHE_CLEANUP

questions.title: What is a transport, and what are workbench and customizing transport requests?
questions.description: In an SAP landscape, development happens in the development system, and changes must be moved to the quality and then the production system in a controlled way. A transport request (managed in transactions SE09 / SE10) is the container that records changed objects and carries them from one system to the next through the Transport Management System (TMS). When you change a transportable object, like a class, a CDS view, or a UI5 app's BSP application, the system asks for a transport request, and the object is recorded in your task inside it. When the work is finished, you release your task and then the request; it is exported, and imported into the next system, usually after testing and approval. There are two main types. A workbench request transports repository objects (development): ABAP code, dictionary objects, CDS views, OData services, UI5 apps. These are cross-client, so after import they are available in all clients of the target system. A customizing request transports client-specific configuration, like the settings made in the IMG (SPRO) or entries in customizing tables, for example company codes or launchpad configuration for one client. Choosing the right type, and keeping related changes in the same or properly ordered requests, avoids broken imports. A request contains tasks, one per developer; each developer releases their task, then the request is released and imported with STMS. A UI5 app is a BSP application, a repository object, so it always goes into a workbench request. Launchpad content depends on its scope: content created in the customizing scope (/UI2/FLPD_CUST) goes into a customizing request, while content in the configuration scope (/UI2/FLPD_CONF) is cross-client and goes into a workbench request. Deploying an app with its tiles and target mappings therefore often needs both kinds, imported in the right order, or the app exists but no tile points to it. Two things that go wrong: an object created in $TMP was never added to a transport (it works in DEV and is missing in QAS), and transports imported in the wrong order reference something that does not exist yet. Import return codes: 0 = fine, 4 = warnings, 8 = errors, 12 = fatal. Useful transactions: SE09/SE10 (transport organizer), STMS (import queues and routes), SE80, SICF, SEMOBJ (semantic objects), LPD_CUST, SU01.
keyPoints: A transport request records changed objects and moves them from development to quality to production (TMS).
Objects are recorded in a task; release the task, then the request, which is then imported into the next system.
Workbench request: repository objects (code, CDS, OData services, UI5 apps); cross-client.
Customizing request: client-specific configuration (IMG/SPRO, customizing tables).
UI5 app = workbench; launchpad content: CUST scope = customizing request, CONF scope = workbench (cross-client).
Return codes: 0 ok, 4 warnings, 8 errors, 12 fatal. Watch $TMP objects and import order.

examples.title: A transport request's life
examples.code:
S4DK900123  Workbench request  "Product app: discount field"
  └─ Task S4DK900124 (developer)
       ├─ R3TR WAPA ZPRODUCTS        (BSP application = the UI5 app)
       └─ R3TR DDLS Z_C_PRODUCT      (CDS view)

1. Develop in DEV -> 2. release task -> 3. release request
4. import into QAS, test -> 5. import into PRD
